lesson.title: Mitosis: Splitting One Nucleus Into Two
lesson.summary: Mitosis is the process by which a cell's replicated chromosomes are separated into two genetically identical nuclei, using a repurposed cytoskeleton to physically move and divide the genetic material.
lesson.body:
Mitosis is the process by which a cell divides its nucleus, distributing the duplicated chromosomes it prepared during interphase into two nuclei that are genetically identical to each other and to the original. It is conventionally described in four sequential stages, prophase, metaphase, anaphase, and telophase, each of which accomplishes a distinct part of the job. Mitosis itself is division of the nucleus specifically; the division of the rest of the cell's contents into two separate cells, called cytokinesis, typically begins during the later stages of mitosis and finishes shortly after it.

None of this would be physically possible without the cytoskeleton. In animal cells, microtubules radiating out from structures called centrosomes near the two ends of the cell assemble into the mitotic spindle, the apparatus that physically attaches to chromosomes and pulls them apart. This is the same microtubule system that, in a non-dividing cell, helps maintain cell shape and moves organelles around, temporarily repurposed for the specific job of chromosome segregation. Microfilaments, built from actin, take on their own essential role slightly later, forming the contractile ring that carries out cytokinesis and physically pinches one cell into two.

The four phases of mitosis, previewed briefly here and covered in full detail next, each handle one piece of this process. In prophase, the duplicated chromosomes condense into compact, visible structures and the spindle begins to form. In metaphase, the spindle aligns every chromosome along the cell's center. In anaphase, the sister chromatids that make up each chromosome are finally pulled apart and moved to opposite ends of the cell. And in telophase, two new nuclear envelopes form around the two separated sets of chromosomes, essentially undoing what prophase did.

Mitosis is how multicellular organisms grow from a single fertilized cell into trillions of cells, and it is how tissues replace cells lost to normal wear, injury, or programmed turnover. It is also how many single-celled eukaryotic organisms reproduce asexually. In every case, the outcome is the same: one cell becomes two cells carrying identical genetic instructions.
